summary: Extends SCTP so an endpoint can tell its peer to move the cumulative ack point forward, giving a partially reliable service to upper layers. It adds a new parameter to INIT and INIT ACK and a new FORWARD TSN chunk. It also gives one example of such a service.

plainLanguage.summary: The SCTP extension lets a sender stop trying to deliver a message and tell its peer to skip past it. Applications can use this when fresh data is more useful than delayed data.

questions: how does sctp partial reliability work
what is timed reliability in sctp
subtitle: SCTP can let an application abandon messages that are no longer useful.

tldr.problem: Reliable SCTP keeps retransmitting lost data, even when an application would prefer to move past a stale message.
tldr.mechanism: Peers negotiate Forward-TSN support. A sender that abandons data can send a FORWARD TSN chunk to move the receiver's cumulative acknowledgment point.
tldr.outcome: Applications can combine reliable and partially reliable messages in one SCTP association. The RFC defines timed reliability as one service.

facts.label: Maximum recommended FORWARD TSN delay
facts.value: SHOULD NOT exceed 200 ms; MUST NOT exceed 500 ms

today: RFC 3758 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2004. The work-unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Partial Reliability Helps
sections.content:
Base SCTP reliably retransmits data. Some applications also send time-sensitive messages for which an old value is less useful than a newer one.

Partial Reliable SCTP (PR-SCTP) lets an application choose, for each message, how long the sender should try to deliver it. One association can carry both fully reliable and partially reliable data while using SCTP's normal congestion control.
sections.plainLanguage: Some messages must arrive, while others lose value if delayed. PR-SCTP lets an application choose whether the sender should keep trying for each message.

sections.title: Negotiating Forward-TSN Support
sections.content:
An endpoint advertises support with the optional Forward-TSN-Supported parameter in INIT and INIT ACK. Both endpoints must support the feature before the association can use it.

If an endpoint did not advertise support, it must not send or process FORWARD TSN during that association. It treats a received FORWARD TSN as unsupported.
sections.plainLanguage: Both endpoints signal support during association setup. If either side does not support the extension, neither side may use it.

sections.title: The FORWARD TSN Chunk
sections.content:
The new FORWARD TSN chunk has type 192 (0xC0). It carries a New Cumulative TSN, telling the receiver to treat missing transmission sequence numbers up to that point as received.

For ordered data, the chunk also lists stream identifiers and the highest skipped stream sequence number. The receiver uses those values to release data waiting behind an abandoned message in a stream's reordering queue.
sections.plainLanguage: The chunk names the point the receiver should skip to. It can also identify ordered stream messages that are no longer coming.

sections.title: Sender and Receiver Processing
sections.content:
The sender tracks an advanced acknowledgment point. When it abandons a chunk, it treats it as no longer outstanding but does not count it as acknowledged for congestion-window growth. If a fragmented message is abandoned, all its fragments are abandoned together.

The sender sends FORWARD TSN when the advanced point passes the peer's reported cumulative acknowledgment. The receiver advances its point, releases stranded ordered data, and drops incomplete messages that can no longer be completed. A skipped chunk arriving later is treated as a duplicate.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender tells the receiver which missing data it will no longer retransmit. The receiver advances past that data and can deliver later ordered messages.

sections.title: Timed Reliability
sections.content:
The RFC defines timed reliability as an example service. In base SCTP, a message first sent before its lifetime expires remains reliable. With timed reliability, the sender may also abandon the message after that lifetime expires.

Before assigning a TSN and before each send or retransmission, the sender checks the message lifetime. If it has expired, the sender abandons the message and may notify the upper layer. The application MUST NOT change the lifetime after passing the message to SCTP.
sections.plainLanguage: A message can have a lifetime. Once it expires, the sender stops retransmitting it and moves on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the extension adds no security concerns beyond those of SCTP, while sharing the issues of unordered data described in RFC 3436. A man-in-the-middle can already change or withhold SCTP data.

FORWARD TSN does not create a new attack, but it can make selective skipping easier for a man-in-the-middle because less state is needed.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker in the middle can already withhold data. The skip message can make it easier to skip selected messages when the feature is enabled.
